items.title: Use It or Lose It: The Year-End Money Deadlines Worth Checking Before December 31
items.body:
With roughly two months left in 2026, now is a practical time to review a handful of money deadlines that fall on or near December 31. Some can cost you real money if missed, while others are optional but useful. This guide covers which ones matter, who they apply to, and which are most often overlooked.

*This article is general information, not tax, legal or financial advice. Rules vary by plan and personal situation, so confirm details with your plan administrator, the IRS, or a qualified professional.*

## 1. Flexible Spending Accounts (FSAs): Check Your Plan's Rules

A health care FSA lets you set aside pre-tax money for eligible medical expenses. The classic drawback is the "use it or lose it" rule: money left unspent at the end of the plan year may be forfeited.

Employers can soften that rule in one of two ways, but they are not required to offer either:

- **Carryover:** Some plans let you roll over a limited amount into the next year. The IRS adjusts the maximum carryover annually, so check the current figure with your plan.
- **Grace period:** Some plans give you extra time, up to two and a half months, to incur new expenses against last year's balance.

A plan may offer one of these options, but not both. Many employers offer neither.

**What to do now:**

- Log in to your FSA portal and check your remaining balance and your plan's deadline.
- Find out whether your plan uses a carryover, a grace period, or nothing.
- Look at the claims run-out deadline. Even if you incur an expense on time, you usually must submit the claim by a set date.
- Spend wisely. Eligible items often include prescription copays, dental work, vision exams and glasses, and many over-the-counter products. Check your plan's eligibility list before buying.

Dependent care FSAs follow their own rules and often do not allow carryover, so check them separately.

## 2. Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs)

If you hold a traditional IRA or most employer retirement plans, the government eventually requires you to start withdrawing money. These withdrawals are called required minimum distributions.

Under current federal law, the starting age depends on your birth year. It is 73 for many people today and rises to 75 for those born in 1960 or later. Confirm your own age requirement with the IRS or a tax professional.

Key points:

- **The annual deadline is generally December 31.** Your first RMD is the exception: you may delay it until April 1 of the following year. Delaying means you take two distributions in one calendar year, which can push you into a higher tax bracket.
- **Missing an RMD carries a penalty.** The excise tax on a missed amount has been reduced in recent years, but it is still significant. The IRS may waive it if you show reasonable cause and correct the shortfall promptly.
- **Calculations are done per account type.** Traditional IRAs can often be aggregated, so you may take the total from one account. Employer plans such as 401(k)s generally must be calculated and withdrawn separately.
- **Inherited accounts have their own rules.** Many beneficiaries must empty inherited retirement accounts within a set number of years, and some must also take annual distributions. This area is complicated and frequently misunderstood.

Roth IRAs do not require withdrawals during the original owner's lifetime.

**Commonly missed:** People who have several accounts, who recently changed custodians, or who inherited an account sometimes overlook one of them. Ask each custodian whether an RMD is due and what amount they calculated.

## 3. Charitable Giving

Donations made by December 31 may count toward your 2026 tax year, but the benefit depends on whether you itemize deductions.

Points to consider:

- **Itemizing vs. the standard deduction.** Most households take the standard deduction, which means a cash gift may not reduce taxes unless your total itemized deductions exceed it. Recent law changes have affected how charitable deductions work for different filers, so review the current rules for 2026.
- **Timing counts.** Generally, a gift is dated when you hand it over, for example when a check is mailed or a card charge is processed. Do not wait until the last day, since processing delays can push a gift into the next year.
- **Keep records.** Save receipts or written acknowledgments, especially for larger gifts. Confirm that the organization is a qualifying charity.
- **Appreciated assets.** Donating stock or other assets you have held for more than a year can sometimes let you avoid capital gains tax on the appreciation. Transfers take time, so start early.
- **Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs).** If you are old enough (generally 70½ or older), you can send money directly from an IRA to a charity. A QCD can count toward your RMD while keeping the amount out of your taxable income. The money must go directly from the IRA to the charity.
- **Donor-advised funds.** These let you make a gift in one year and recommend grants to charities later, which can help you bunch several years of giving into one tax year.

## 4. Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)

HSAs differ from FSAs in one important way: the money generally stays yours and does not expire at year end. However, some HSA-related deadlines still matter.

- **Eligibility.** You can contribute only if you are covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan and have no disqualifying other coverage.
- **Contribution limits.** The IRS sets annual limits for self-only and family coverage, with an additional catch-up amount for those 55 and older. Check the 2026 figures before you contribute.
- **Deadline.** Unlike many year-end items, you can usually make contributions for the tax year until the tax filing deadline the following April. Payroll contributions, however, must go through your employer during the year.
- **Don't overfund.** Contributing above the limit, including employer contributions, can trigger a tax penalty unless corrected.
- **Last-month rule.** In certain cases, being eligible in December can allow a full-year contribution, but it comes with a testing period. Understand the conditions before relying on it.

## 5. Other Deadlines Worth a Quick Look

- **Open enrollment.** Many employer benefit elections, including FSA and HSA amounts, are set during open enrollment. Mark the deadline for choosing 2027 benefits.
- **Retirement plan contributions.** Contributions to a 401(k) generally have to be made through payroll by December 31, while IRA contributions can usually be made until the filing deadline in April. Check whether you are on track to reach your contribution goal and whether your employer match is fully captured.
- **Tax-loss harvesting.** Investors with taxable accounts sometimes sell losing positions to offset gains. Be aware of the wash-sale rule, which can disallow a loss if you buy back a substantially identical investment too soon.
- **Gift tax annual exclusion.** Gifts to individuals up to the annual limit generally do not require a gift tax return. The exclusion does not carry over to the next year.
- **Estimated taxes.** If you have freelance, business or investment income, review whether you have paid enough during the year to avoid underpayment penalties.
- **Insurance and plan reviews.** Check beneficiary designations, since outdated ones can override what you intend.

## A Simple Year-End Checklist

1. **This week:** Check FSA balances and your plan's carryover or grace-period policy.
2. **By mid-November:** Confirm whether you owe an RMD and contact each custodian.
3. **By early December:** Decide on charitable gifts and start any stock transfers.
4. **Before December 31:** Make final payroll contribution changes where possible, and complete RMDs and any FSA spending.
5. **In January:** Gather tax documents and plan your HSA and IRA contributions for the prior year.

## Bottom Line

Not every deadline applies to everyone. The costliest mistakes tend to be the quiet ones: a forgotten FSA balance, a missed RMD on a lesser-used account, or a donation that is processed too late. A short review in the next few weeks can help you avoid unpleasant surprises. When in doubt, check with your plan administrator or a tax professional, since limits and rules change from year to year.

items.title: The Lame-Duck Session: What Congress Must Finish After the Midterms
items.body:
Every two years, American voters head to the polls for the midterm elections, and the results reshape the balance of power in Washington. But the new Congress does not take office the morning after Election Day. Instead, there is a gap of roughly two months in which the outgoing members remain in charge. This stretch is known as the **lame-duck session**, and it often decides how the next year begins.

## What Is a Lame-Duck Session?

A lame-duck session is any meeting of Congress after the November election but before the new term starts on January 3. The name comes from the idea of a "lame duck," an official whose time in office is ending. Some members in the session have lost their races, some have chosen to retire, and others won re-election and will simply continue. All of them still hold full legislative power until the old Congress officially ends.

Under the 20th Amendment, ratified in 1933, the terms of members of Congress begin on January 3. Before that change, the old Congress could linger until March, which left a long stretch of time when lawmakers who had been voted out still made decisions. Moving the date earlier shortened the lame-duck period, but did not remove it.

## Why the Calendar Creates Pressure

Congress rarely finishes everything before the campaign season. Lawmakers spend much of the autumn at home, talking with voters. When they return in November, a long list of unfinished tasks is waiting, and a hard deadline sits at the end of the year. Several kinds of business tend to pile up.

### Government Funding

The most common item is funding for federal agencies. The government's fiscal year starts on October 1, and Congress is supposed to pass spending bills by then. In practice, lawmakers often pass a short-term measure called a **continuing resolution**, which keeps agencies running at current levels for a limited time. When that measure expires in the weeks after the election, Congress must act again. The options usually include:

- Passing a full-year set of spending bills.
- Combining many bills into one large package, often called an omnibus.
- Passing another temporary extension to push the decision into the new year.

If none of these succeeds, parts of the government can face a shutdown, which delays services and creates uncertainty for federal workers and contractors.

### Expiring Policies

Many laws are written with end dates. Tax provisions, health programs, and other policies may be set to lapse at the end of a year or a fiscal period. Lawmakers often use the lame-duck session to extend, change, or let them expire. Because these deadlines are firm, they can become a reason to move legislation that might otherwise stall.

### Nominations and Other Business

The Senate may also spend time confirming judges and executive branch officials before the balance of the chamber changes. In addition, Congress sometimes handles annual defense policy legislation, disaster relief, and other must-pass items during this window.

## How the Election Results Change the Mood

The tone of a lame-duck session depends heavily on the election outcome. If control of one or both chambers is about to change hands, the party that is losing power may try to finish priorities while it still can. The party gaining power may prefer to wait, hoping to write the terms of major bills itself in January. This often leads to a choice between two paths:

1. **Finish the work now**, which gives certainty but may reflect the priorities of the outgoing majority.
2. **Delay until the new Congress**, which lets the incoming majority shape the outcome but risks another funding cliff early in the year.

When party control does not change, the session may be calmer, though disagreements over spending levels and policy details can still produce tense negotiations.

## Why Critics and Supporters Disagree

The lame-duck session draws debate about fairness and accountability. Critics argue that lawmakers who were just rejected by voters should not make major decisions, because they no longer face the same electoral pressure. Supporters respond that members remain duly elected officials until their terms end, and that deadlines leave Congress with little choice but to act. They also note that the lack of immediate election pressure can sometimes make compromise easier.

## Why It Matters for the Year Ahead

What happens in these few weeks can set the stage for the coming year. A completed funding package can give agencies stability and clear the new Congress to focus on other priorities. A deal that is pushed forward, on the other hand, can mean that the first months of the new term are spent on the same deadlines the previous Congress could not resolve. Decisions on expiring policies also shape what households, businesses, and state governments can expect.

## What to Watch For

For readers following the process, a few signals are useful:

- **The funding deadline.** Check when the current short-term measure ends, since that date drives much of the schedule.
- **Package size.** A large combined bill suggests leaders want to clear the table before January.
- **Leadership statements.** Comments from congressional leaders often reveal whether they plan to finish business or wait.
- **The list of expiring provisions.** The number and importance of these items show how much pressure lawmakers face.

## The Bottom Line

The lame-duck session is a short but important stretch of the political calendar. It connects the voters' verdict in November with the work of a new Congress in January, and it reminds us that governing does not pause after the votes are counted. Understanding how it works makes it easier to follow the news, and to see why a few weeks at the end of the year can influence much of what follows.

*This article is for general informational purposes and does not represent the position of any party or candidate.*

items.title: [International Logistics #8] When Your Cargo Gets Damaged at Sea, Who Pays and How Much?
items.body:
> The amount you can recover from an ocean carrier for lost or damaged cargo depends on which international rulebook applies, and the gap between rulebooks can be thousands of dollars.

## Today's Concept

Every year, containers fall overboard, take on seawater, or arrive with crushed contents. When that happens, the cargo owner usually asks the obvious question: *the carrier was supposed to deliver it safely, so isn't the carrier responsible?*

The answer is "partly, under conditions, and only up to a limit." Ocean shipping has its own liability regime, mostly set by international conventions. Each one strikes a different balance between **carriers** (shipping lines) and **shippers** (cargo owners). Three are worth knowing.

**1. The Hague-Visby Rules (1968, built on the 1924 Hague Rules)**
This is the most widely used regime among major trading nations. The carrier must exercise **due diligence to make the ship seaworthy** before and at the start of the voyage, and must take proper care of the cargo. In exchange, the carrier gets a long list of defenses. The best known is the **"nautical fault" exception**: if the loss comes from the crew's error in navigating or managing the ship, the carrier is generally not liable. Fire is also a defense unless the carrier itself was at fault. Liability is capped at **666.67 SDR per package or 2 SDR per kilogram, whichever is higher**. The SDR (Special Drawing Right) is an IMF currency basket worth roughly US$1.30–1.40. Claims must be brought within **one year**.

**2. The Hamburg Rules (1978, in force 1992)**
These were pushed largely by cargo-owning and developing countries that felt Hague-era rules favored shipowners. The Hamburg Rules **remove the nautical fault exception**, presume the carrier is at fault unless it proves otherwise, raise the limits to **835 SDR per package or 2.5 SDR per kg**, cover **delay**, and extend the time bar to **two years**. Most major shipping and trading nations never joined, so their practical reach is limited.

**3. The Rotterdam Rules (2008)**
This is a modern attempt to replace both. They cover **door-to-door** transport when a sea leg is involved, recognize **electronic transport records**, require seaworthiness to be maintained **throughout the voyage** (not just at the start), drop the nautical fault exception, and raise limits to **875 SDR per package or 3 SDR per kg**. However, they need 20 ratifications to take effect and have received only a handful, so **they are not yet in force**.

In short, over time the rules have moved toward more carrier responsibility and higher limits. In practice, though, the older rules still govern most cargo.

## In Everyday Life

Picture a small furniture retailer in Ohio importing a container of dining sets from Shanghai through the Port of Los Angeles. One crate arrives water-damaged, and the goods inside were worth $12,000.

The United States never adopted Hague-Visby, Hamburg, or Rotterdam. U.S. ocean shipments run under the **Carriage of Goods by Sea Act (COGSA, 1936)**, which is based on the original 1924 Hague Rules. Its limit is **$500 per package** (or per "customary freight unit"), and that figure has not been adjusted for inflation since 1936.

If the bill of lading lists that crate as one package, the retailer's recovery from the carrier may be capped at **$500**, even if the carrier is clearly at fault. Two ways around this:

- **Declare a higher value** on the bill of lading (usually for an extra freight charge), or
- **Buy cargo insurance**, which is what most experienced importers do.

One practical tip: how the packages are counted on the bill of lading matters. Listing "1 container" and listing "40 cartons" can lead to very different limits.

## 3-Line Summary

1. Ocean carriers are liable for cargo loss or damage, but only under conditions and up to per-package or per-kg limits.
2. Hague-Visby is the most widely used regime and keeps the nautical fault defense. Hamburg and Rotterdam are more shipper-friendly, but Hamburg has limited reach and Rotterdam isn't in force yet.
3. U.S. shipments fall under COGSA's $500-per-package limit, so declaring a value or buying insurance is essential.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** Under the Hague-Visby Rules, a carrier is generally NOT liable for cargo damage caused by the crew's error in navigating the ship. (O/X)

**Q2.** Which regime is designed to cover door-to-door transport and electronic transport records?
- A) Hague Rules
- B) Hamburg Rules
- C) Rotterdam Rules
- D) COGSA

**Q3.** A U.S. importer ships goods worth $20,000 as a single package under COGSA without declaring a value. What is the carrier's maximum liability, as a rule?
- A) $20,000
- B) $5,000
- C) $500
- D) Nothing at all

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Carrier:** The party that contracts to transport goods, typically the shipping line.
- **Seaworthiness:** The condition of a ship being properly built, equipped, crewed, and fit to carry its cargo safely.
- **Nautical fault exception:** A Hague/Hague-Visby defense that excuses the carrier for losses caused by the crew's errors in navigating or managing the ship.
- **Limitation of liability:** The legal cap on what a carrier must pay, usually set per package or per kilogram.
- **SDR (Special Drawing Right):** An IMF reserve asset based on a basket of major currencies, used to set limits in international transport conventions.

---

*Answers: Q1 – O. The nautical fault exception is the best-known carrier defense under Hague-Visby, and both the Hamburg and Rotterdam Rules remove it. Q2 – C. The Rotterdam Rules cover "maritime plus" door-to-door carriage and recognize electronic records, though they are not yet in force. Q3 – C. COGSA limits liability to $500 per package unless a higher value is declared on the bill of lading, which is why cargo insurance is so common.*

items.title: Buy Now, Pay Later Meets the Holidays: Is Split-Pay Shopping Easing Budgets or Hiding Debt?
items.body:
As the holiday shopping season ramps up, a growing number of shoppers are choosing to split purchases into smaller installments instead of paying all at once. "Buy now, pay later" (BNPL) options now appear at the checkout of many online retailers and, increasingly, in physical stores. For some households, they make a big season of gifts and travel easier to manage. For others, they raise a harder question: when payments are spread across several plans and providers, is it still easy to see how much you owe?

This article explains how these loans generally work, why they can be hard to track, and what lenders and regulators are paying attention to as spending picks up. It is general information, not financial advice.

## How split-pay plans typically work

BNPL products come in a few common forms. Details vary by provider, retailer, and the shopper's profile, so always read the terms shown at checkout.

- **Pay-in-four plans.** The purchase is divided into four equal payments. The first is usually due at checkout, and the rest follow every two weeks. Many of these plans carry no interest when payments are made on time.
- **Longer monthly installment loans.** Larger purchases may be spread over several months or longer. These loans may charge interest, and the rate can depend on the shopper's credit profile.
- **Card-linked or wallet-based installments.** Some payment apps and card issuers now let users convert a purchase into installments after the fact.

Approval is often quick and may involve only a light credit check. That speed is a big part of the appeal. It is also part of why the products draw scrutiny.

## Why shoppers like them

- **Smoother cash flow.** Splitting a cost across several paychecks can make a large holiday expense easier to fit into a monthly budget.
- **Predictable schedules.** A fixed payment calendar can feel simpler than a revolving credit card balance.
- **Potential cost savings.** When payments are made on time, many pay-in-four plans charge no interest, which can compare favorably with carrying a credit card balance.

## Why the debt can be hard to see

The same features that make BNPL convenient can make it easy to lose track of.

1. **Many small obligations.** A shopper might use one provider for clothing, another for electronics, and a third for travel. Each plan has its own due dates, and no single statement shows them all.
2. **Limited visibility in credit reports.** Reporting practices have varied by provider. Some plans have not been consistently reflected in traditional credit files, which means lenders may not see the full picture of a borrower's commitments. Reporting practices continue to evolve, so check how your own providers handle it.
3. **Payments hit at the wrong time.** Installments from holiday purchases can land in January and February, when many households are also dealing with credit card bills and other post-holiday costs.
4. **Spending can feel smaller than it is.** A $60 payment is easier to approve mentally than a $240 purchase. Several of them together can add up quickly.
5. **Fees and overdrafts.** Late fees, where they apply, and failed automatic payments can create costs that were not part of the original plan. Payments pulled automatically from a bank account can also trigger overdraft charges if the balance runs low.

## What lenders and regulators are watching

As usage has grown, financial institutions and public agencies have been looking more closely at the BNPL market. Specific rules differ by jurisdiction and continue to change, but several themes come up repeatedly:

- **Disclosure.** Whether shoppers are clearly told the total cost, the payment schedule, and any fees before they commit.
- **Consumer protections.** Questions about how disputes, returns, and refunds are handled when a purchase is paid for through an installment provider.
- **Credit reporting.** How, and whether, installment loans should be reported so that lenders can assess a borrower's overall debt load.
- **Underwriting.** How providers decide who qualifies, especially when approval takes seconds and the credit check is limited.
- **Stacking.** Lenders and analysts watch for borrowers who hold several plans at once, since overlapping payments can raise the risk of missed payments.

Card issuers and banks, for their part, have been adding or expanding their own installment features, and many are paying closer attention to how these obligations affect repayment behavior across a customer's accounts.

## Practical steps for holiday shoppers

If you plan to use split-pay options this season, a few habits can help keep things manageable:

- **Make a list.** Write down every active plan, the amount, and the due dates. A simple spreadsheet or calendar reminder works.
- **Set a total ceiling.** Decide how much you can comfortably repay each month, then count all installments toward that number.
- **Check the terms.** Look for interest, late fees, and what happens if a payment fails.
- **Time payments to paydays.** If you can choose a due date, line it up with when income arrives.
- **Keep a cushion.** Make sure the linked bank account or card can cover automatic payments.
- **Know the return process.** Understand how refunds work for items bought through an installment plan.
- **Ask whether you would buy it at full price.** If the answer is no, the installment option may only be hiding the cost.

## The bottom line

Split-pay shopping can be a useful tool when it is used deliberately, with a clear view of what is owed and when. It can also make spending feel lighter than it really is, especially when several plans overlap. As the holiday season builds, the key question for shoppers is not only whether they can afford each individual payment, but whether they can afford all of them together, and whether they are tracking them closely enough to know.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, legal, or investment advice. Consider consulting a qualified professional about your personal situation.*
